category: Adjectives that only follow a verb

examples: The kids were afraid of the dog next door.
He was too afraid to move.
As a kid, I was more afraid of the dark than of anything else.
She was afraid that nobody would show up.
He's afraid of losing his job.
We were afraid for our daughter when the storm hit.
I'm afraid we're out of the large size.
"Is it serious?" "I'm afraid so."
I'm afraid I can't make it on Friday.
He's not afraid of hard work.
Don't be afraid to ask questions.
She's never been afraid to speak her mind.

senses.head: Feeling fear of someone or something
examples: The kids were afraid of the dog next door.
He was too afraid to move.
As a kid, I was more afraid of the dark than of anything else.

senses.head: Worried that something bad will happen, or worried about someone's safety
examples: She was afraid that nobody would show up.
He's afraid of losing his job.
We were afraid for our daughter when the storm hit.

senses.head: I'm afraid: used to say politely that something is unwelcome or disappointing
examples: I'm afraid we're out of the large size.
"Is it serious?" "I'm afraid so."
I'm afraid I can't make it on Friday.

senses.head: not afraid of, not afraid to: willing to do or face something hard, unpleasant or unpopular
examples: He's not afraid of hard work.
Don't be afraid to ask questions.
She's never been afraid to speak her mind.

entries.position: predicative only — also after a noun when it has its own phrase (a kid afraid of the dark); before a noun use frightened or scared: a frightened child
entries.takes: of + noun or -ing (what you fear); for + person (fear for their safety); to-infinitive; that-clause
entries.form: a- adjective, from an old participle
entries.contrast: Never directly before a noun: a frightened child, a scared dog, not an afraid child. Afraid of + -ing is fear that something will happen (afraid of falling); afraid to + verb is being too scared to do it (afraid to jump). Afraid for is fear on someone else's behalf (afraid for her son). I'm afraid often has nothing to do with fear: it softens bad news, like Russian боюсь, что or к сожалению, and the short answers are I'm afraid so and I'm afraid not. Strengthen it with very, really or terribly, not much.

examples: Is the fish still alive?
He was lucky to be alive after the crash.
At 97, she's the oldest woman alive in the county.
The family keeps the old traditions alive.
The team's playoff hopes are still alive.
I've never felt more alive than on that trip.
She really comes alive on stage.
The neighborhood is most alive after dark.
The pond was alive with frogs.
By nine o'clock the streets were alive with music.
The mayor seems fully alive to the risks.
Good teachers are alive to every student's needs.

senses.head: Living; not dead
examples: Is the fish still alive?
He was lucky to be alive after the crash.
At 97, she's the oldest woman alive in the county.

senses.head: Still existing or in use; not forgotten or lost
examples: The family keeps the old traditions alive.
The team's playoff hopes are still alive.

senses.head: Full of energy, interest and feeling
examples: I've never felt more alive than on that trip.
She really comes alive on stage.
The neighborhood is most alive after dark.

senses.head: alive with: full of moving things, sounds or activity
examples: The pond was alive with frogs.
By nine o'clock the streets were alive with music.

senses.head: alive to: aware of something and ready to act on it
examples: The mayor seems fully alive to the risks.
Good teachers are alive to every student's needs.

entries.position: predicative only — also right after a noun (the happiest man alive) or an object (keep hope alive); before a noun use living or live: living things, live lobsters
entries.comparison: more/most — more alive, most alive, in the 'full of energy' sense
entries.takes: with + noun (full of); to + noun (aware of)
entries.form: a- adjective, from Old English on life
entries.contrast: Never before a noun: a live fish (/laɪv/) or a living animal, not an alive fish. Russian живой splits three ways: alive after a verb (The fish is still alive), live before a noun for animals, music and broadcasts (live music, a live broadcast), and lively for a person or place full of energy (a lively kid, a lively bar). Living describes people and languages that exist now (living relatives, a living language). Alive with means full of (alive with birds); alive to means aware of.

examples: Were you alone in the house last night?
I need to be alone for a while.
The two of them were alone in the elevator.
After the divorce, she felt completely alone.
I've never felt more alone than in that huge city.
If you're struggling with this, you're not alone.
She was alone in thinking the plan would fail.
You alone can make that decision.
The shipping alone costs fifty dollars.
Leave your brother alone!
Leave the thermostat alone — I just set it.

senses.head: Without other people; by yourself
examples: Were you alone in the house last night?
I need to be alone for a while.
The two of them were alone in the elevator.

senses.head: Feeling lonely and without support
examples: After the divorce, she felt completely alone.
I've never felt more alone than in that huge city.

senses.head: Being the only person who has a certain feeling, view or problem — often in not alone
examples: If you're struggling with this, you're not alone.
She was alone in thinking the plan would fail.

senses.head: Right after a noun or pronoun: only; and nobody or nothing else
examples: You alone can make that decision.
The shipping alone costs fifty dollars.

senses.head: leave alone: not bothered, touched or changed by anyone
examples: Leave your brother alone!
Leave the thermostat alone — I just set it.

entries.position: predicative only — also right after a noun or pronoun in the sense 'only' (you alone, the fee alone); before a noun use lone or solitary: a lone rider
entries.comparison: more/most — more alone, most alone, in the 'lonely' sense; for emphasis all alone
entries.takes: with + person (nobody else there); in + noun or -ing (the only one who thinks or feels so)
entries.contrast: Never before a noun: a lone traveler or a woman on her own, not an alone woman. Alone means with nobody else and can be neutral or even pleasant (I like being alone); lonely means sad about it and goes in both positions (a lonely old man). In She lives alone and He did it alone the word is an adverb. Let alone is a fixed phrase meaning 'and certainly not' (I can't boil an egg, let alone cook dinner), Russian не говоря уже о. Leave me alone is оставь меня в покое, not literally оставь меня одного.

examples: Don't make any noise — the baby's asleep.
I fell asleep on the couch watching TV.
By the time we got home, the kids were fast asleep.
I can't stand up yet — my foot is asleep.
My arm fell asleep during the movie.
The regulators were asleep at the switch while the bank took huge risks.
Our defense was asleep on that play.

senses.head: Sleeping
examples: Don't make any noise — the baby's asleep.
I fell asleep on the couch watching TV.
By the time we got home, the kids were fast asleep.

senses.head: Of an arm, leg, hand or foot: numb from staying in one position
examples: I can't stand up yet — my foot is asleep.
My arm fell asleep during the movie.

senses.head: Not paying attention when you should be; not reacting — often asleep at the wheel or asleep at the switch
examples: The regulators were asleep at the switch while the bank took huge risks.
Our defense was asleep on that play.

entries.position: predicative only — before a noun use sleeping: a sleeping baby
entries.comparison: not gradable — strengthen with fast, sound or half: fast asleep, half asleep
entries.contrast: Never before a noun, and not very asleep: a sleeping child, sound asleep. Russian заснуть is fall asleep (the moment), спать is be asleep (the state), and ложиться спать is go to bed or go to sleep: I fell asleep at ten, At ten I was already asleep. Sleepy is сонный — wanting to sleep, not sleeping. My foot is asleep is the everyday way to say a leg or arm has gone numb (затекла).

examples: Are you still awake?
I lay awake half the night worrying about the test.
Two cups of coffee and I'm wide awake.
I feel much more awake after a shower.
Nobody is fully awake at a 7 a.m. meeting.
Few people were awake to the risks back then.
Parents are finally awake to the dangers of vaping.

senses.head: Not sleeping
examples: Are you still awake?
I lay awake half the night worrying about the test.
Two cups of coffee and I'm wide awake.

senses.head: Alert and able to think clearly; not sleepy
examples: I feel much more awake after a shower.
Nobody is fully awake at a 7 a.m. meeting.

senses.head: awake to: aware of something and ready to deal with it
examples: Few people were awake to the risks back then.
Parents are finally awake to the dangers of vaping.

entries.position: predicative only — before a noun use a relative clause: children who are still awake
entries.form: a- adjective, related to the verb wake
entries.contrast: Awake is the state; wake up is the change: I woke up at six (проснулся), but I was awake at six (не спал). Awake (awoke, awoken) and awaken (awakened) are also formal verbs, but everyday American English uses wake up. Strengthen the adjective with wide or fully (wide awake). Stay awake is не спать, and lie awake is лежать без сна.

examples: Are you aware of the new parking rules?
I'm aware that the deadline is tight.
People are much more aware of the risks than they used to be.
I suddenly became aware of someone standing behind me.
She was aware of a strange smell in the kitchen.
Young voters today are very politically aware.
We want to raise an environmentally aware generation.

senses.head: Knowing that something exists or is happening
examples: Are you aware of the new parking rules?
I'm aware that the deadline is tight.
People are much more aware of the risks than they used to be.

senses.head: Noticing something through your senses at the moment it happens
examples: I suddenly became aware of someone standing behind me.
She was aware of a strange smell in the kitchen.

senses.head: Informed about and interested in a subject — usually after an adverb such as politically or environmentally
examples: Young voters today are very politically aware.
We want to raise an environmentally aware generation.

entries.position: predicative only — also after a noun with its own phrase (people aware of the risks); before a noun only with an adverb in front: a politically aware student
entries.takes: of + noun or -ing; that-clause; how, what, who and other wh-clauses
entries.contrast: The preposition is of, not about: aware of the problem. Be aware is the state (знать, быть в курсе); become aware or realize is the moment you notice. Well aware stresses that someone knows perfectly well (I'm well aware of that). Before a noun aware needs an adverb (an environmentally aware company); an aware person sounds odd — say an informed person. Conscious overlaps in the 'knowing' sense but also means в сознании, which aware never does.

examples: You should be ashamed of yourself.
He was ashamed that he had lied to his parents.
I've never been more ashamed of my own behavior.
I'm ashamed to admit that I've never read it.
She was too ashamed to ask for help.

senses.head: Feeling guilty or embarrassed because of something you did, or because of someone or something connected with you
examples: You should be ashamed of yourself.
He was ashamed that he had lied to his parents.
I've never been more ashamed of my own behavior.

senses.head: Unwilling to do something because you feel shame
examples: I'm ashamed to admit that I've never read it.
She was too ashamed to ask for help.

entries.position: predicative only — before a noun use shamefaced or embarrassed: a shamefaced grin
entries.takes: of + noun, -ing or yourself; to-infinitive; that-clause
entries.form: old past participle of the verb ashame; the -ed is /d/, not /ɪd/
entries.contrast: Ashamed is guilt about something wrong or bad (ashamed of lying); embarrassed is awkwardness about something silly or public (embarrassed when I tripped). Russian стыдно covers both, so choose carefully: I'm ashamed after spilling coffee on your boss sounds far too strong. Ashamed to + verb means you do not want to do it because of shame (too ashamed to ask). Shameful describes the act (shameful behavior), and It's a shame means жаль, not стыдно.

examples: My brother and I are nothing alike.
No two snowflakes are exactly alike.
The twins look more alike every year.
entries.position: predicative only — needs a plural subject or look alike; before a noun use similar or identical: similar houses
entries.contrast: Alike joins two or more things and takes no preposition: The sisters are alike, not She is alike her sister. For one thing compared with another use like or similar to (She is like her sister). Never before a noun: similar cars, not alike cars. In teachers and students alike and treat everyone alike the word is an adverb meaning 'equally'. A lookalike is a noun (двойник).

examples: Within minutes the whole warehouse was ablaze.
Rioters set two police cars ablaze.
The hills were ablaze with fall colors.
The stadium was ablaze with lights.
Her eyes were ablaze with anger.
The whole town was ablaze with excitement before the big game.

senses.head: Burning strongly
examples: Within minutes the whole warehouse was ablaze.
Rioters set two police cars ablaze.

senses.head: Very bright with lights or colors
examples: The hills were ablaze with fall colors.
The stadium was ablaze with lights.

senses.head: Full of strong feeling or excitement
examples: Her eyes were ablaze with anger.
The whole town was ablaze with excitement before the big game.

entries.position: predicative only — also after an object (set the barn ablaze); before a noun use blazing or burning: a burning building
entries.contrast: Mostly written and news English; in speech Americans say on fire: The car was on fire. Never before a noun: a burning car, not an ablaze car. Set something ablaze is the same as set fire to something. The figurative senses take with: ablaze with lights, eyes ablaze with anger.

examples: The fishermen were adrift for three days before a Coast Guard helicopter found them.
The storm snapped the rope, and the canoe was adrift.
After college, I felt completely adrift.
Laid-off workers were left adrift with no plan for retraining.

senses.head: Of a boat or a person at sea: floating without being steered or tied to anything
examples: The fishermen were adrift for three days before a Coast Guard helicopter found them.
The storm snapped the rope, and the canoe was adrift.

senses.head: Without direction, purpose or support
examples: After college, I felt completely adrift.
Laid-off workers were left adrift with no plan for retraining.

entries.position: predicative only — also after an object (cast adrift, set adrift); before a noun use drifting: a drifting boat
entries.contrast: Never before a noun: a drifting raft, not an adrift raft. Cast adrift and set adrift mean to leave someone or something with no control or support. In British sports reports adrift means behind (five points adrift); Americans say behind. Russian дрейфовать is the verb drift: The boat drifted, or The boat was adrift.

examples: The boat was damaged but still afloat.
She grabbed a cooler to keep herself afloat.
The restaurant barely stayed afloat during the pandemic.
A second job kept us afloat that year.
Rumors were afloat that the coach would quit.
There are a lot of wild theories afloat right now.

senses.head: Floating on water; not sinking
examples: The boat was damaged but still afloat.
She grabbed a cooler to keep herself afloat.

senses.head: Having enough money to keep operating or to pay your bills
examples: The restaurant barely stayed afloat during the pandemic.
A second job kept us afloat that year.

senses.head: Of a rumor or idea: going around; being talked about
examples: Rumors were afloat that the coach would quit.
There are a lot of wild theories afloat right now.

entries.position: predicative only — also after an object (keep the boat afloat); before a noun use floating: a floating dock
entries.contrast: Never before a noun: a floating log, not an afloat log. Russian на плаву fits both main senses (keep a company afloat). In the money sense the usual verbs are stay, keep and remain. Float is the verb (Wood floats); afloat describes the state.

examples: Her parents were aghast at the size of the bill.
We watched, aghast, as the bridge collapsed.
Fans were aghast when the team traded its best player.
entries.position: predicative only — also set off by commas (She stared, aghast); before a noun use horrified or shocked: a horrified look
entries.form: old past participle of agast 'to frighten'; the h is silent
entries.contrast: Formal and written; in conversation say horrified or shocked. The preposition is at: aghast at the news, not aghast of. Never before a noun: a shocked crowd, not an aghast crowd.

entries.meaning: Similar to something; of the same kind. ---
examples: What she felt was akin to panic.
Learning a language is akin to learning a musical instrument.
The meeting was more akin to a pep rally than a planning session.
entries.position: predicative only — also right after a noun (something akin to panic)
entries.contrast: Formal; in speech say like or similar to. The preposition is always to: akin to, not akin with. Never before a noun. Russian сродни is a close match in both meaning and register.

entries.meaning: Strongly disliking or opposed to something. ---
examples: My dad is averse to paying for anything he can fix himself.
Older investors tend to be more averse to risk.
I'm not averse to a little hard work.
entries.position: predicative only — before a noun only in compounds: risk-averse investors
entries.contrast: Do not confuse with adverse (harmful, both positions): adverse effects, adverse weather. Averse describes a person who dislikes something: averse to risk. It takes to + -ing, not an infinitive: not averse to working late. It most often appears as not averse to, a polite way of saying не прочь: I'm not averse to a second helping. Before a noun use the compound: a risk-averse company.

examples: He's perfectly content with his small apartment.
After years of moving around, she finally seems content.
I've never been more content than I am now.
I'm content to let the lawyers handle it.
She was content to stay in the background.

senses.head: Happy and satisfied with what you have, and not wanting more
examples: He's perfectly content with his small apartment.
After years of moving around, she finally seems content.
I've never been more content than I am now.

senses.head: Willing to accept or do something, even if it is not ideal
examples: I'm content to let the lawyers handle it.
She was content to stay in the background.

entries.position: predicative only — before a noun use contented: a contented smile
entries.contrast: The adjective is stressed on the second syllable, /kənˈtɛnt/, like the verb (content yourself with). The noun content (содержание, контент) is /ˈkɑːntɛnt/, stressed on the first. Before a noun use contented: a contented cat, not a content cat. Content is quieter than happy: it means you want nothing more, Russian довольный. Content to + verb means willing to accept something, not delighted by it.

examples: I'm so glad you could make it.
I'm really glad for you two.
I've never been gladder to see anyone in my life.
I'd be glad to help you move.
If you need a ride, I'm glad to drive.
I was glad of the extra blanket that night.
She was glad of the company on the long drive.
The Christmas card promised glad tidings to all.
The old hymn tells of a glad morning.

senses.head: Pleased and happy about something
examples: I'm so glad you could make it.
I'm really glad for you two.
I've never been gladder to see anyone in my life.

senses.head: Very willing to do something
examples: I'd be glad to help you move.
If you need a ride, I'm glad to drive.

senses.head: Grateful for something
examples: I was glad of the extra blanket that night.
She was glad of the company on the long drive.

senses.head: Before a noun, in old or literary set phrases: bringing or showing joy
examples: The Christmas card promised glad tidings to all.
The old hymn tells of a glad morning.

entries.position: predicative only — except in a few literary set phrases (glad tidings); before a noun use happy or pleased: a happy face
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — gladder, gladdest; also more glad
entries.takes: about + thing; for + person (glad for someone); that-clause; to-infinitive; of + noun (grateful for)
entries.contrast: Glad reacts to a particular event (I'm glad you came); happy also describes a lasting state and goes before a noun (a happy kid, not a glad kid). I'd be glad to is a polite yes, like Russian с радостью. Glad for someone is рад за кого-то; glad of something means grateful to have it. Gladder and gladdest exist, but more glad is common too.

entries.meaning: Not able to do something, because you lack the power, skill, time or opportunity. ---
examples: I was unable to sleep after the phone call.
The airline was unable to find my bag.
We regret that we are unable to offer refunds.
entries.position: predicative only — always followed by a to-infinitive; before a noun use a relative clause: people who are unable to work
entries.contrast: Unable always needs to + verb: unable to sleep, not unable of sleeping — that pattern belongs to incapable of + -ing. It is more formal than can't or couldn't and is the usual word in notices and emails (We are unable to process your request). The noun is inability, not unability. For a lasting physical or mental condition American English says disabled, not unable.

entries.meaning: Not knowing about something, or not noticing it. ---
examples: Most customers are unaware of the fee.
He was unaware that anyone was listening.
She kept dancing, blissfully unaware of the stain on her dress.
entries.position: predicative only — also set off by commas (She kept dancing, unaware); before a noun use unsuspecting: unsuspecting tourists
entries.comparison: not gradable — strengthen with completely, totally or blissfully
entries.contrast: The preposition is of, not about: unaware of the change. Do not confuse it with the adverb unawares, used in catch or take someone unawares (застать врасплох). Blissfully unaware is a common phrase for someone happily ignorant of a problem.

examples: I've grown very fond of my neighbors.
She's especially fond of old movies.
Absence makes the heart grow fonder.
My uncle is fond of telling everyone how he once met the president.
Politicians are fond of quoting that line.
She gave her son a fond smile.
I have fond memories of those summers at the lake.
Some of my fondest memories are from that camp.
Her fondest wish was to see all her grandkids graduate.
He had the fond hope that the problem would just go away.
Their fond belief that prices would keep rising proved wrong.

senses.head: fond of: liking someone or something, often after knowing them for a long time
examples: I've grown very fond of my neighbors.
She's especially fond of old movies.
Absence makes the heart grow fonder.

senses.head: fond of doing: in the habit of doing something, often something other people find annoying
examples: My uncle is fond of telling everyone how he once met the president.
Politicians are fond of quoting that line.

senses.head: Before a noun: loving and affectionate, or pleasant to remember
examples: She gave her son a fond smile.
I have fond memories of those summers at the lake.
Some of my fondest memories are from that camp.

senses.head: Of a hope, wish or belief: deeply felt and long held, often naively, when it is unlikely to come true
examples: Her fondest wish was to see all her grandkids graduate.
He had the fond hope that the problem would just go away.
Their fond belief that prices would keep rising proved wrong.

entries.position: both — but in the 'liking' sense only after a verb (She's fond of cats); before a noun it means affectionate (a fond smile) or, of a hope, unlikely (a fond hope)
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — fonder, fondest; also more fond
entries.contrast: Be fond of is softer than love and warmer than like, and it takes of + noun or -ing, never an infinitive: fond of cooking, not fond to cook. The meaning changes with position: She's fond of her grandfather means she likes him, but a fond look is a loving one, and a fond hope is a cherished and often naive one. Grow fond of is the usual way to say you came to like someone. The noun is fondness.

examples: I'm really sorry I'm late.
She said she was sorry for what she'd said.
Nobody was sorrier than Mike when the vase broke.
I'm so sorry about your dad.
We were sorry to hear that you'd been sick.
I'm sorry I didn't take that job when I had the chance.
Don't buy that car — you'll be sorry.
I'm sorry, but you can't park here.
I'm sorry, I didn't catch your name.
I'm sorry to say the store is closing.
I feel really sorry for the new kid.
Stop feeling sorry for yourself.
The old house was in a sorry state.
That's the sorriest excuse I've ever heard.
After the frost, the garden was a sorry sight.

senses.head: Feeling regret or guilt about something you did; apologizing
examples: I'm really sorry I'm late.
She said she was sorry for what she'd said.
Nobody was sorrier than Mike when the vase broke.

senses.head: Feeling sad or sympathetic about something bad that happened to someone else
examples: I'm so sorry about your dad.
We were sorry to hear that you'd been sick.

senses.head: Disappointed about a situation or regretting a choice, when no apology is involved — often you'll be sorry
examples: I'm sorry I didn't take that job when I had the chance.
Don't buy that car — you'll be sorry.

senses.head: Used politely to refuse, disagree, give bad news or ask someone to repeat something
examples: I'm sorry, but you can't park here.
I'm sorry, I didn't catch your name.
I'm sorry to say the store is closing.

senses.head: feel sorry for: feeling pity for someone
examples: I feel really sorry for the new kid.
Stop feeling sorry for yourself.

senses.head: Before a noun: poor, pitiful or in bad condition
examples: The old house was in a sorry state.
That's the sorriest excuse I've ever heard.
After the frost, the garden was a sorry sight.

entries.position: both — after a verb for the feelings (I'm sorry); before a noun it means pitiful or poor (a sorry state)
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — sorrier, sorriest; also more sorry
entries.takes: about + thing; for + what you did, or + person you pity; to-infinitive; that-clause
entries.contrast: Sorry about goes with a situation (sorry about the mess, sorry about your dad); sorry for goes with your own action (sorry for yelling) or, after feel, with a person you pity (I feel sorry for him, мне его жалко). I'm sorry to hear is sympathy; I'm sorry to say introduces bad news. Before a noun the meaning changes: a sorry excuse is a poor one, not an apologetic one. To get a stranger's attention use Excuse me, not Sorry — Russian извините covers both. A standalone Sorry! or Sorry? is an interjection.

examples: The ring is worth about $5,000.
How much is your car worth?
Our house is worth twice what we paid for it.
The museum is well worth a visit.
Is it worth fixing, or should we just buy a new one?
It was a long drive, but it was totally worth it.
By forty she was worth over a billion dollars.
Nobody knows exactly how much he's worth.

senses.head: Having a certain value in money
examples: The ring is worth about $5,000.
How much is your car worth?
Our house is worth twice what we paid for it.

senses.head: Good, useful or enjoyable enough to justify the time, money or effort
examples: The museum is well worth a visit.
Is it worth fixing, or should we just buy a new one?
It was a long drive, but it was totally worth it.

senses.head: Of a person: owning money and property of a certain value
examples: By forty she was worth over a billion dollars.
Nobody knows exactly how much he's worth.

entries.position: predicative only — also right after a noun with its complement (a book worth reading, a ring worth $5,000); before a noun use worthwhile or valuable: a worthwhile trip
entries.comparison: not gradable — strengthen with well, really or definitely: well worth it
entries.takes: a noun, amount or pronoun (worth $50, worth it); -ing (worth seeing) — never a to-infinitive
entries.contrast: Worth must have something after it: The book is worth reading, not worth to read and not worth being read — the active -ing carries the passive meaning. Russian стоит + infinitive becomes it's worth + -ing: It's worth trying (стоит попробовать). Worth it stands in for the rest: Was the trip worth it? Before a noun use worthwhile (a worthwhile project); worthy of means deserving (worthy of respect). Because it takes an object, Merriam-Webster and some grammars call worth a preposition. The noun worth is a separate word: a dollar's worth, self-worth.
